analysis.one_liner: Raises estate and gift taxes on large fortunes, with a 77% rate on billion-dollar estates.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rein in the estate tax, which now applies to only a small share of the largest inheritances. It raises rates sharply on the biggest estates — 77% on everything above $1 billion — and lowers the amount any estate can pass on tax-free from roughly $11 million back to $3.5 million. It also closes a series of techniques wealthy families use to shrink their taxable estates, while carving out larger protections for family farms and donated conservation land.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary federal taxpayers benefit if the added revenue funds public priorities, since the tax falls almost entirely on families with estates above $3.5 million — a group that makes up well under 1% of all estates. Family farmers and landowners who donate conservation easements also get larger protections. Heirs who don't stand to inherit nine- and ten-figure sums gain nothing directly but benefit from a tax code whose largest avoidance channels are narrowed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal taxpayers; not the largest estates

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a 77% marginal tax rate on the portion of any estate, gift, or generation-skipping transfer above $1 billion, with rates of 39% to 55% below that.
It lowers the basic exclusion amount — the sum that can pass to heirs tax-free — from its current level to $3.5 million, restoring the tax to a larger share of very large estates.
It increases the special reduction in the value of qualifying farmland for estate tax purposes from $750,000 to $3 million, adjusted for inflation, easing the burden on family farms.
It raises the maximum estate tax exclusion for donated conservation easements from $500,000 to $2 million.

It closes several estate-tax avoidance channels: it limits valuation discounts on family minority stakes in businesses, tightens rules for grantor retained annuity trusts, subjects grantor trusts to transfer tax at death, eliminates the generation-skipping exemption for trusts designed to last more than 50 years, and requires consistent value reporting for gifts and transfers in trust.

analysis.who_pays: Families with estates over $3.5 million pay higher estate tax, and households with billion-dollar fortunes pay the 77% top marginal rate. Wealthy families relying on long-duration dynasty trusts, grantor trusts, GRATs, and minority-interest valuation discounts lose those techniques. Estates and gift-givers also face new reporting requirements on the value of transferred assets.

drawbacks.text: Lowering the exclusion to $3.5 million means estates well short of billionaire scale — larger family businesses, investment portfolios, and high-value property in expensive regions — would face the 39% and 45% brackets, not just the ultra-wealthy.

The bill is a pure revenue measure: it raises money for the Treasury without designating any particular use, so its benefit to ordinary people depends entirely on how a future Congress spends the revenue.
The new disclosure requirements would force executors and gift-givers to file statements identifying the value of every interest transferred, adding compliance paperwork for large estates and gifts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is heavily progressive: the burden lands on the top fraction of one percent of estates, and the bill explicitly shields family farms (a $3 million land valuation break) and conservation donations, which addresses the most common good-faith objection to estate tax increases. The real costs are the wider reach into estates between $3.5 million and the current higher exemption, and the added paperwork — real but modest compared to the revenue at stake.

outcome.mechanism: Sanders introduced it in January 2019 and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a markup or vote; the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Sen. Sanders on January 31, 2019, and read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
That referral was the bill's last action of record; the Finance Committee took it up no further and it never reached the Senate floor.
One Democratic senator cosponsored the bill; no other members of either party joined.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The wealthiest estates came out ahead: billion-dollar family fortunes and dynasty trusts kept the current, lower estate tax and the avoidance techniques the bill would have eliminated. Trust and estate planners kept their business, and the Treasury forfeited the projected revenue from the largest inheritances.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured its referral to the Finance Committee.

for.name: Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only senator from either party to do so.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or hearing on the bill, leaving it without action after referral for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No roll call was ever held, so no vote pattern exists; the bill's only recorded supporters were Sanders and one Democratic cosponsor, and no Republican senator signed on.

industries.note: The bill would impose a 77% marginal rate above $1 billion and strip the tax exemption from trusts engineered to last beyond 50 years, directly reducing the wealth passed to the largest family fortunes. The public's gain in revenue comes at their expense.

The bill narrows the core techniques the estate-planning business sells — minority-interest valuation discounts, short GRATs, grantor trust sales, and indefinite dynasty trusts — reducing demand for high-end avoidance work.

Lowering the exclusion to $3.5 million pulls in estates that currently owe no estate tax under the roughly $11 million exemption in effect. These families were not the bill's main target but would bear real new tax.

The bill quadruples the special farmland valuation reduction to $3 million, making it easier for working farms to pass intact to the next generation even as the tax reaches further up the wealth scale.
Raising the conservation easement estate-tax exclusion to $2 million strengthens the incentive for landowners to donate development rights, a benefit to conservation groups and public lands.
